items.text: COMMITTEE DISCHARGED AND COMMITTED TO RULES

items.memo:
BILL NUMBER:  S3866

 TITLE OF BILL :
An act to amend the family court act, in relation to evidence in
permanency proceedings in the family court


This is one in a series of measures being introduced at the request of
the Chief Administrative Judge upon the recommendation of her Family
Court Advisory and Rules Committee.

This measure would amend the Family Court Act in relation to the
evidentiary rules to be applicable in Article 10 and 10-A proceedings.

Prior to enactment of landmark permanency legislation in 2005  L.
2005, c. 3 , permanency hearings - and their predecessors, hearings to
extend child protective placements, to review voluntary foster care
placements and to review cases of children freed for adoption - were
commenced by the filing of sworn petitions. As pleadings, these
petitions were automatically part of the records of the proceedings
that were subject to review on appeal. Additionally, hearsay evidence
was admissible in these hearings, pursuant to section 1046 of the
Family Court Act, which required that evidence be competent, not
simply material and relevant, only for child protective fact-finding
hearings. In disposition and all post-dispositional proceedings,
evidence need only be material and relevant. Section 1046, which
applied to all child protective proceedings and freed-child reviews,
contained additional provisions important for permanency hearings,
including, inter alia, provisions permitting entry into evidence of:
(i) certified hospital and social service records of public and
private agencies where Family Court determined that a proper
foundation had been established, and (ii) a child's hearsay statements
to a third party regarding child abuse or neglect; and precluding
assertion of spousal, physician, rape crisis counselor, social worker
and psychologist privileges to exclude otherwise-admissible evidence.

While simplifying permanency proceedings and to provide one unified
article (Family Court Act Article 10-A) consolidating all applicable
provisions, the 2005 legislation inadvertently has created
difficulties. Because permanency reports are not pleadings, they are
not automatically part of the record and Family Courts have differed
as to their admissibility into evidence. Without admitting such
reports into evidence, appellate courts have virtually no documentary
records to review on appeal. As is evident from the extensive
delineation of information required to be included in permanency
reports  Family Court Act §1089(c) , appellate courts would be kept in
the dark as to the various dimensions of child safety, well-being and
permanency planning that comprise the essence of permanency hearings
if permanency reports are not made a part of the formal record.

Further, since section 1046 of the Family Court Act only explicitly
applies to proceedings under Article 10 of the Act, its provisions
have not been extended to apply to permanency hearings under Article
10-A of the Act. There have been cases in which therapists' reports,
which would have been admitted without question in pre-2005
proceedings, have been denied admissibility, and there have been cases
in which courts have taken the position that, in the absence of
statutory authorization, only evidence that is competent may be
admitted in permanency hearings. Such limitations cripple the
permanency hearing process, preventing the courts from exercising the
broad responsibilities imposed upon them by the 2005 legislation, as
well as by the federal and New York State Adoption and Safe Families
Acts  Public Law 105-89; L.1999, c. 7 . Family Court must make
findings regarding the best interests, safety needs of and appropriate
permanency goal for children and may thus need to determine, among
other issues, what progress parents have made in treatment programs
and in other efforts to achieve reunification with their children;
what "reasonable efforts" agencies have made in furthering
reunification or other permanency plans; how children are doing in
school and whether special needs they may have are being met and, in
the case of children 14 years of age and older, what transitional
services may be appropriate; and what the facts and circumstances may
have been in instances in which they have withheld their consents to
adoption. These determinations, as in dispositional hearings in child
protective proceedings, may well require admission of social service
and clinical records, letters from programs, follow-up progress
reports, reports of statements of children regarding abuse and neglect
and other evidence that would be admissible if section 1046 of the
Family Court Act were still applicable to these proceedings.
Additionally, with Family Court retaining continuous jurisdiction over
the cases, the Court may need to convene follow-up proceedings and
entertain requests for interim relief in between permanency hearings
that may be based upon communications from programs, agencies or
clinicians that may constitute reliable hearsay but may not rise to
the level of competent evidence:

We propose this measure to provide a simple solution to these
difficulties. The measure would amend section 1046 of the Family Court
Act to make it explicitly applicable to proceedings under Article
10-A, as well as Article 10, of the Act, and would make a
corresponding amendment to section 1089 of the Act. Further, the
measure would clarify that material and relevant evidence would be
admissible in permanency hearings.

With the protections provided in Article 10-A - continuous
representation of parents and children, requirements for provision of
permanency reports to all counsel, notice and rights to be heard by
foster parents and relatives caring for children and the "one
family/one judge" approach to the assignment of cases - the due
process rights of all parties to test the reliability of all evidence
presented, including permanency reports and any other documents and
testimony, would be protected. Parties could call the makers of
reports to testify, to object to Family Court according weight to
portions of the report or hearsay evidence that may be unreliable, to
object to any evidence not meeting the materiality or relevance
requirements and to present witnesses and documents of their own in
order to refute or amplify issues presented by petitioner agencies in
permanency reports and in their direct cases. So, too, would the
appellate rights of all parties be protected by providing that the
appellate courts would have the benefit of a full record containing
all of the evidence relied upon by the Family Court. Enactment of this
measure is essential to realization of the explicit purposes of
Article 10-A of the Family Court Act as expressed in section 1086 of
the Act, ie., to establish "uniform procedures" in order "to provide
children placed out of their homes timely and effective judicial
review that promotes permanency, safety and well-being in their
lives."

This measure, which would have no fiscal impact upon the State, would
take effect 60 days after becoming a law.

 2008 LEGISLATIVE HISTORY :

S.7343 (passed Senate).

BILL NUMBER:  S3866A

 TITLE OF BILL :  An act to amend the family court act, in relation to

Family Court Act, which required that evidence be competent, not
simply material and relevant, only for child protective fact-finding
hearings. In disposition and all post-dispositions' proceedings,
evidence need only be material and relevant. Section 1046(a), which
applied to all child protective proceedings extensions of placement,
permanency hearings and freed-child reviews, contained additional

provisions permitting entry into evidence of: (i) certified hospital

Act. There have been cases in which therapists' reports, which would
have been admitted without question in pre-2005 proceedings, have been
denied admissibility, and there have been cases in which courts have
taken the position that, in the absence of a statutory provision

admitted in permanency hearings. Such limitations cripple the

and clinical records, letters from programs, follow-up progress
reports, reports of statements of children regarding abuse and neglect
and other evidence that would be admissible if subdivisions (a) and
(e) of section 1046 of the Family Court Act were still applicable to

jurisdiction over the cases, the Court may need to convene follow-up

subdivisions (a) and (c) of section 1046 into Article 10-A by
reference. Further, the measure would clarify that material and
relevant evidence would be admissible in permanency hearings.

With the protections provided in Article 10-A - continuous
representation of parents and children, requirements for provision of
permanency reports to all counsel, notice and rights to be heard by

all of the evidence relied upon by the Family Court. Enactment of this
measure is essential to realization of the explicit purposes of
Article 10-A of the Family Court Act as expressed in section 1086 of
the Act, i.e., to establish "uniform procedures" in order "to provide
children placed out of their homes timely and effective judicial
review that promotes permanency, safety and well-being in heir lives."

This measure, which would have no fiscal impact upon the State, would
take effect 60 days after becoming a law.
